opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think the core issue is that most of the agent stacks we've built so far inherited a very batch-oriented mental model. You send a request, the model thinks, it calls some tools, it comes back with an answer. And that's fine when the world holds still while you're working. But a real-time agent, whether it's a voice agent, something operating a UI, or something sitting in a network control loop, lives in a world that keeps changing underneath it. The user starts talking again halfway through your response. A new event arrives that makes your current plan stale. Some tool call you kicked off is now pointless.

Right now the typical answer is pretty crude: you just kill the generation and start over. That throws away a lot of useful partial work, and it's also kind of unsafe, because you don't really know what state you left things in. Did that API call go through or not? Did you half-write a file? Did you say half a sentence the user already heard and is now reacting to?

So what I mean by a better notion of interruptible work is borrowing ideas that systems people have had for decades: preemption points, checkpoints, transactional or idempotent actions, the idea of distinguishing work that's safe to abandon from work that has to either commit or roll back. If an agent's work is structured that way, then when an interrupt comes in, you can ask, what's the cheapest consistent state I can get to right now? Maybe you keep the retrieval you already did, cancel the speculative tool calls, and fold the new input into the existing context rather than restarting cold.

There's also a latency angle. In real-time settings the thing users feel is responsiveness, and if every interruption means paying full time-to-first-token again plus redoing tool calls, the experience degrades really fast. Being able to resume, or to fork from a checkpoint, is just a much better latency story.

And honestly, I think it's a bit of a modeling problem too, not just infrastructure. Models aren't really trained to think, "I might get cut off at any moment, so let me front-load the important stuff and keep my state legible." Getting both sides right, runtimes that support preemption cleanly and models that behave well under it, is where I think a lot of the interesting work in real-time agents is going to be.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so the way I think about it is that most of the agent frameworks we have today were built with a batch mental model. You give the agent a task, it goes off and runs a loop of tool calls and reasoning, and eventually it comes back with an answer. And that's fine when the human is willing to wait, but it falls apart the moment you put the agent in a real-time setting, like a voice conversation or a live coding session, where the world is changing underneath it while it's working.

The core problem is that the agent treats its work as atomic. Once it starts a tool call or a chain of reasoning, there's no clean way to say "stop, the user just said something that changes everything," and have it gracefully absorb that. Right now you basically have two bad options. You either let it finish, which means it might spend thirty seconds doing something that's now irrelevant, or you kill it, and you lose all the partial state, all the context it built up, and you start over from scratch.

What I think we actually need is something closer to how operating systems think about preemption. Work should have checkpoints. The agent should be able to be interrupted at a well-defined boundary, look at the new information, and decide: do I throw away what I was doing, do I keep going, or do I fold this new thing into my plan? That's a very different design than a for loop that calls tools until it hits a stop condition.

And there's a subtler point here too, which is about the model's own sense of time. When a human is talking to you, they can tell when you're mid-sentence versus when you've reached a natural pause. Agents don't really have that. They don't know which parts of their work are safe to drop and which parts are halfway through a side effect. If you're mid-way through writing a file or sending an API request, interrupting there is genuinely dangerous. So interruptible work isn't just a scheduling problem, it's also about making the agent explicit about where its own safe points are.

I think once you solve that, a lot of the stuff that feels awkward about real-time agents today, the latency, the "hold on, let me finish" moments, the double-handling of user input, a lot of that goes away. The agent starts to feel like a collaborator who's actually listening rather than a process you kicked off and have to wait on.

astra-6.text:
I think it’s because real-time interaction means new information can arrive while you’re still doing something. Someone asks a question, you start working on it, and then they say, “Actually, I meant this other thing.” The agent needs to respond to that without blindly finishing the original task or throwing away everything it’s already done.

So interruptibility is more than stopping the model from generating. It’s knowing what work is in progress, what’s still useful, and whether any action has already happened. You can cancel a calculation, but if you’ve sent a message, stopping the agent doesn’t unsend it.

The useful abstraction is something like: pause this work, incorporate the new information, and decide what to resume or abandon. That’s a big part of making an agent feel responsive—having the user’s latest intent actually change what it’s doing.

sol-6.1.text:
I think because most of our abstractions assume that once you start a piece of work, you want it to finish. But in a real-time conversation, that’s often not true. Someone starts asking a question, you begin looking something up, and then they say, “Actually, never mind, I meant this other thing.” The work you were doing may already be irrelevant.

And interrupting isn’t just stopping the audio. You need to decide what happens to the underlying work. Do you cancel the search? Keep the result around because it might still be useful? And if you’ve started an action with a side effect, can you safely stop it?

So I think agents need a more explicit notion of which work is speculative, which work is still relevant, and where they’re committing to something. That lets them respond to a person changing direction without either throwing everything away or blindly finishing an obsolete task.
